summaries.example: Imagine a music player app. A person wants it to play songs in a certain way. That wish is an intention. The rules for what the app must do are its specification. A programmer then writes an algorithm, or step-by-step plan, and turns it into code. The code is stored on a phone, and the phone’s physical parts carry out the instructions. These layers work together, even though we often call the instructions “software” and the phone’s parts “hardware.”
summaries.summary: The philosophy of computer science asks what computer systems are and how we can understand them. A common picture separates software, such as programs and algorithms, from hardware, such as processors and storage devices. The entry explains that this separation is useful in everyday work, but it may not describe two completely independent kinds of things. Every program needs some physical form, and what one person calls software may be treated as hardware at another level of work. A different picture describes a computer system through levels of abstraction. These levels can begin with a person’s goal, continue through requirements, an algorithm, programming-language instructions, machine code, and end with the physical execution of the instructions. Each level gives meaning and requirements to another level. Abstraction lets people work with a manageable amount of detail, but it does not erase the details that lower levels must implement. This layered view helps explain why computer science studies not only machines and code, but also the relationships among goals, instructions, designs, and physical actions.
key_ideas: Computer systems include both instructions and physical machinery, but the boundary between software and hardware is not always perfectly sharp.
Computer scientists can study a system at several levels, from a person’s goal to code and finally to the machine running the code.
Abstraction hides some details without making them disappear; lower levels still have to handle those details.
A system is not fully understood by looking at only one level. The levels work together.
summaries.why_it_matters: The way we describe a computer system affects how we design it, test it, and decide whether it is working correctly. Thinking in layers helps people find where a problem began: in the goal, the instructions, the code, or the machine. It also shows why a computer system is more than a pile of parts or a list of commands.

important_terms.definition: A machine or set of parts that takes information, follows instructions, and produces results.
The instructions and patterns used by a computer, such as an app or program.
The physical parts of a computer, such as its processor, memory, and storage.
A step-by-step plan for completing a task.
A description of what a computer system is required to do.
A way of looking at one part of a complicated system while setting aside some details.

questions_to_think_about: Is an app only the code, or does it also need a physical device to exist?
When is it helpful to ignore details? When could ignoring them cause a problem?
Could two different programs carry out the same task?
What might happen if the instructions are right but a computer part breaks?

summaries.example: Suppose a school commissions an app to block unwanted calls. The users’ goal is an intention: prevent calls from selected sources. A specification turns that goal into requirements, such as maintaining a list, checking each incoming number, and allowing or blocking the call according to the list. An algorithm gives a procedure for meeting those requirements. Source code expresses that procedure in a high-level language; a compiler translates it into lower-level instructions; and a processor executes those instructions physically. summaries.summary: The philosophy of computer science investigates the ontology and methodology of computational systems: what such systems are, how their parts relate, and how their behavior can be specified, implemented, verified, and judged correct. One influential description divides systems into software and hardware. Software is associated with algorithms, source code, and programs, while hardware includes processors, storage, and other physical machinery. The entry surveys challenges to treating this as a strict ontological division. Programs have physical realizations, and the same item may be classified differently at different stages of design and engineering. Other proposals describe software as both abstract and concrete, or as an abstract artifact. A broader approach uses levels of abstraction. In one formulation, a system can be followed from intention, through specification, algorithm, high-level language, assembly or machine instructions, and execution. Each level serves as a functional description for lower levels and as a structural realization for higher ones. Abstraction makes complex systems manageable, but computational abstraction differs from simply discarding information: implementation details remain necessary at lower levels. This framework connects the nature of computational systems with implementation and correctness. It also opens wider debates about physical computation and about whether computer science is best understood through mathematical proof, engineering practice, empirical testing, or a combination of these methods.
key_ideas: The software–hardware distinction is practically useful, but philosophical accounts disagree about whether it marks a fundamental difference in what exists.
A layered ontology includes intention, specification, algorithm, high-level code, machine code, and execution; no single layer exhausts the identity of the computational system.
Computational abstraction conceals implementation details while preserving a dependence on implementation. Hidden information is not simply destroyed.
Implementation and correctness are related: a lower level is correct when it realizes the relevant requirements of a higher level.
The philosophy of computer science examines both ontological questions about systems and methodological questions about specification, programming, verification, and testing.
The entry presents competing views about whether computer science is primarily mathematical, engineering-based, scientific, or a combination of these approaches.
summaries.why_it_matters: These distinctions influence real judgments about whether a system has met its requirements. A mathematically correct program can still run incorrectly because of a physical fault; conversely, a working program may solve the wrong problem if its specification fails to express users’ intentions. Philosophical analysis clarifies why verification, testing, abstraction, and system design answer different questions rather than providing one universal test of correctness.

important_terms.definition: The study of what computational systems are, how they are structured, and how claims about their behavior can be justified.
The branch of philosophy asking what kinds of things exist; here, it concerns the entities and relations making up computational systems.
A layered way of describing a system by selecting which features matter at a particular level.
A formally or informally stated set of requirements that determines which behaviors count as acceptable.
A procedure or set of instructions for solving a class of problems under stated conditions.
The relation in which a lower level realizes or instantiates requirements expressed at a higher level.
The property of satisfying the requirements imposed by a relevant higher level, such as a specification.
A human-made object or system designed to fulfill functions; computational systems can include both abstract and physical artifacts.

questions_to_think_about: Does the software–hardware distinction describe two different kinds of entities, or mainly two practical viewpoints?
If two programs have different code but perform the same function, in what sense might they be the same or different?
Why can testing reveal a bug without proving that no bugs remain?
Can a physical system count as computational merely because an observer can describe it using computational terms?
How should user goals and changing contexts affect judgments of correctness?

summaries.example: Suppose students design an app that sorts homework reminders. Their first idea—“help us remember assignments”—is an intention. They turn it into a specification: the app must accept subjects and due dates, sort tasks by date, and display the next task. An algorithm explains the steps for sorting. Programmers write those steps as source code, which is translated into machine instructions and carried out by the phone. The same system can be discussed at each level. A mistake in the sorting plan, a bug in the code, or a broken phone part could all lead to a wrong result, but they would be different kinds of problems.
summaries.summary: The philosophy of computer science asks questions about the nature of computer systems and the methods used to build and understand them. One familiar approach divides a system into software and hardware. Programs, algorithms, and source code are usually treated as software, while processors, drives, and machines are treated as hardware. The entry explains why this division is useful but not perfectly sharp. A program always has some physical realization, and the category called software can shift when people examine a system from another professional viewpoint. Philosophers have therefore proposed other ways to describe these entities. The levels-of-abstraction approach treats a computational system as a hierarchy. It may begin with an intention about a problem, followed by a specification of requirements, an algorithm, high-level programming instructions, machine-level instructions, and physical execution. Each level hides some features while depending on lower-level implementation. This is important because a system cannot be defined completely by only its code, only its hardware, or only its user’s goal. The layered picture also explains why correctness is connected with implementation: every level must properly realize the requirements supplied by relevant higher levels. These questions lead into larger debates about algorithms, programs, physical computation, verification, testing, and the place of computer science among mathematics, engineering, and empirical science.
key_ideas: Philosophers disagree about whether software and hardware are truly separate kinds of things or mainly useful categories for different jobs.
The levels-of-abstraction approach describes computing as a connected stack, including goals, requirements, algorithms, code, machine instructions, and execution.
Abstraction makes a problem easier to handle, but the details set aside at one level still matter at lower levels.
Specifications help determine correctness, while implementations explain how requirements are realized.
A failure can begin at different levels, so finding a bug is not always the same as finding the deeper cause of a system’s problem.
summaries.why_it_matters: Everyday technology depends on many layers working together. A specification can be unclear, an algorithm can be unsuitable, code can contain a bug, or hardware can malfunction. Understanding the layers helps developers and users describe problems more accurately and avoid treating one kind of success—such as passing a test—as proof that the whole system is correct.

important_terms.definition: A computer-based arrangement that receives information, changes or uses it according to instructions, and produces behavior or results.
The nonphysical-looking side of computing, including programs, source code, and algorithms; philosophers debate how separate it really is from hardware.
The physical machinery that stores or carries out instructions, including processors and memory.
A clear series of steps for solving a type of problem, often designed to finish and produce a result.
Requirements that say what a system must do and provide standards for judging its behavior.
Studying a system at a chosen level while leaving some details for other levels to handle.
The process by which one level of a system realizes the requirements described at another level.
A human-made object or system designed to perform a function.

questions_to_think_about: Why might a programmer and a circuit designer classify the same part of a computer differently?
Does a program exist if every physical copy and record of it disappears?
How can two different algorithms both be correct solutions to one problem?
Why does a successful test not prove that a program has no bugs?
Should a system be judged only by its written specification, or also by what users need it to do?
